text-decoration 文本装饰 none, underline, line-through text-decoration: none;（去除链接下划线）

文本排版

属性 ** 描述** 常用值 示例
text-align 水平对齐 left, center, right, justify text-align: center;
text-indent 首行缩进 em, px text-indent: 2em;（缩进 2 个字符）

font 简写

将多个字体属性合并为一条声明（顺序：style → weight → size/line-height → family）：

权重计算：

盒模型

盒模型组成

一个盒子由四部分组成（从内到外）：

  • Content（内容）：实际内容（文本、图片）
  • Padding（内边距）：内容与边框之间的空间
  • Border（边框）：围绕内边距的线条

CSS 性能优化建议

  • 重置默认样式：使用 * { margin: 0; padding: 0; box-sizing: border-box; } 或 Normalize.css 确保跨浏览器一致性。
  • 复用类名：优先使用类选择器而非 ID 选择器，提高可复用性。
  • 移动优先：先为移动端设计，再通过媒体查询适配大屏幕。
  • **避免 !important**：过度使用会破坏优先级机制——仅在紧急情况下使用。
  • 优化性能：使用字体图标/雪碧图替代多张图片；尽量简化选择器复杂度。

entry.content:

Introduction

Hello everyone, this is Alex. As we know, a tree is a frequently-used data structure to simulate a hierarchical tree structure.One reason to use trees might be because you want to store information that naturally forms a hierarchy.

Also there are some other applications using trees:

    1. Manipulate hierarchical data.
    1. Make information easy to search (see tree traversal).
    1. Manipulate sorted lists of data.
    1. As a workflow for compositing digital images for visual effects.
    1. Router algorithms
    1. Form of a multi-stage decision-making (see business chess).

A Binary Tree is one of the most typical tree structure. I have posted [Binary Tree] which include some significant information definitions and manipulation of [Binary Tree]. Please check it before viewing this article. Here are some common Binary Tree Leetcode problems I have sorted them out.

By completing these problems, you will be able to:

    1. Deeply understand the concept of a binary tree;
    1. Be familiar with different traversal methods;
    1. Use recursion to solve binary-tree-related problems;

Introduction to Recursion
The process in which a function calls itself directly or indirectly is called recursion and the corresponding function is called a recursive function.

  • A recursive algorithm takes one step toward solution and then recursively call itself to further move. The algorithm stops once we reach the solution.
  • Since called function may further call itself, this process might continue forever. So it is essential to provide a base case to terminate this recursion process.

Steps to Implement Recursion:

Step 1:Determine the parameters and return values of recursive functions
Parameters are pointers to the nodes that need to be passed in, and no other parameters are needed. Usually, the main parameters are set at this time. If other parameters are found to be needed in writing recursive logic, they can be added at any time.
In fact, there is no need to return a value, but the pointer given in the question to return the root node can be directly used with the function defined in the question, so the return type of the function is TreeNode.

Step 2:Determine termination conditions
When the current node is empty then return.

Each recursive call allocates a new Stack Frame in the Call Stack to store the local variables, parameters, and return address of the current function. If there is no termination condition, recursion will continue indefinitely, stack frames will pile up infinitely, and eventually exceed the JVM’s stack space limit —> leading to Stack overflow Error.

Step 3:Determine the logic of single-layer recursion
It’s very important to detremine what the logic of single-layer recursion: 4. Tree Traversal Techniques(Tree Traversal Techniques) like PreOder, PostOrder and InOrder to solve the problem respectively.

entry.title: 常见二叉树问题
entry.content:
1. 引言
  2. 案例研究
    • 翻转二叉树
    • 对称二叉树
    • 二叉树的最大深度
    • 二叉树的最小深度
    • 完全二叉树的节点个数
    • 平衡二叉树
    • 二叉树的所有路径
    • 左叶子之和
    • 找树左下角的值

引言

大家好，我是 Alex。众所周知，树（Tree）是一种常用的数据结构，用于模拟层次化的树状结构。使用树的一个原因是，你可能需要存储天然具有层次关系的信息。

此外，树还有一些其他应用：

    1. 操作层次化数据。
    1. 使信息易于搜索（参见树的遍历）。
    1. 操作已排序的数据列表。
    1. 作为视觉特效中数字图像合成的工作流。
    1. 路由算法。
    1. 多阶段决策模型（参见博弈树）。

二叉树（Binary Tree）是最典型的树结构之一。我之前发布过 [二叉树]，其中包含了二叉树的一些重要概念、定义和基本操作。在阅读本文之前请先查看那篇文章。以下是我整理的常见二叉树 LeetCode 题目。

完成这些题目后，你将能够：

    1. 深入理解二叉树的概念；
    1. 熟悉不同的遍历方式；
    1. 使用递归解决二叉树相关问题；

递归简介
函数直接或间接调用自身的过程称为递归（Recursion），相应的函数称为递归函数。

  • 递归算法每一步都向解靠近一步，然后递归调用自身继续前进。一旦到达解，算法就停止。
  • 由于被调用的函数可能进一步调用自身，这个过程可能会无限进行下去。因此，必须提供一个基本情况（base case）来终止递归过程。

实现递归的步骤：

步骤 1：确定递归函数的参数和返回值
参数是需要传入的节点指针，不需要其他参数。通常在此时设置主要参数。如果在编写递归逻辑时发现需要其他参数，可以随时添加。
实际上不需要返回值，但题目中要求返回根节点的指针，可以直接使用题目中定义的函数，因此函数的返回类型为 TreeNode。

步骤 2：确定终止条件
当前节点为空时直接返回。

每次递归调用都会在调用栈（Call Stack）中分配一个新的栈帧（Stack Frame），用于存储当前函数的局部变量、参数和返回地址。如果没有终止条件，递归将无限进行下去，栈帧会无限堆积，最终超出 JVM 的栈空间限制 —> 导致 栈溢出（Stack overflow） 错误。

步骤 3：确定单层递归的逻辑
确定单层递归的逻辑非常重要：4. Tree Traversal Techniques（树的遍历技巧），如 前序遍历（PreOrder）、后序遍历（PostOrder） 和 中序遍历（InOrder） 分别用来解决问题。

entry.title: Building AI Agents: From Context to Memory
entry.content:
• Introduction
  • What Is an AI Agent
    • The Core Formula: LLM + Context + Tools
    • The ReAct Loop: How Agents Actually Work
  • Context Engineering: The Ceiling of Agent Capability
    • Context at the API Level: Static Prefix + Dynamic Trajectory
    • KV Cache: Why Prefix Stability Matters
    • Prompt Engineering: Writing the Agent’s Operating Manual
    • Agent Skills: Load Knowledge On Demand
    • Agent Status Bar: From Implicit State to Explicit Knowledge
    • Context Compression: When Less Is More
  • From Context to Memory: Making Agents Remember
    • User Memory: Building a Model of the User
    • Four Storage Formats: From Simple Notes to Advanced JSON Cards
    • RAG: Giving Agents a Knowledge Base
    • Beyond Flat Text: Structured Indexing and Agentic RAG
    • Contextual Retrieval: Fixing Chunking at the Root
    • The Two-Tier Memory Architecture
  • Harness Engineering: Reliability Beyond the Demo
    • Constrain, Verify, Correct: The Three Safety Layers
    • Workflow vs. Autonomous: Choosing the Right Pattern
  • Best Practices
  • FAQ
  • Summary

Introduction

If you have used Cursor to write code and watched it search your codebase, edit multiple files, and rerun tests until they pass, you have already used an AI Agent. The same is true if you have used Deep Research to investigate a topic through repeated searching and reading, or had Manus control a browser to finish online tasks.

These products take many forms, but they share a common trait: they are no longer passive “you ask, it answers” conversations. They plan their own execution steps, call the tools each task requires, and adjust their strategy as results come in.

This article walks through the core ideas behind modern AI Agents, from the foundational formula, to context engineering within a single session, to persistent memory across sessions. The goal is to give you a mental model you can use to build your own agents.

What Is an AI Agent

The Core Formula: LLM + Context + Tools

The essence of a modern Agent system fits into one concise formula:

Agent = LLM + Context + Tools

Each term is broader than it first appears:

  • The LLM is the reasoning engine. It is the decision-making core, responsible for understanding intent, reasoning, planning, and judgment. Its capabilities come from world knowledge acquired during pre-training, plus decision-making strategies encoded through post-training.
  • Context is the working set of information. Not just the text fed into the model, but everything available at each decision point—the environment, user memory, domain knowledge, the agent’s own state, and task progress.
  • Tools are the action interfaces. The full set of ways the agent can act—from predefined tool calls to skills loaded on demand, from generating code to delegating work to sub-agents.

Put more intuitively: Agent = Reasoning Engine + Working Context + Action Interfaces. The model reasons and decides, the context provides the information those decisions depend on, and the tools provide the interfaces through which decisions affect the outside world.

Different kinds of agents compare across these three dimensions:

Agent Product Working Context Action Interfaces Strategy
Coding Agents (Cursor) Requirements, codebase, terminal Code search, file read/write, command execution Understand → search → edit → test → debug
Search Agents (Deep Research) Web resources, databases Search queries, web reading, summary generation Iterative deepening based on existing information
Computer Control (Manus) Screen, browser, file system Clicking, typing, scrolling, screenshots Visual perception + operation
Phone Assistants (Doubao) Phone screen, installed apps Clicking, swiping, opening apps Intent understanding + app control
Task Agents (Pine AI) Account info, historical bills Making calls, sending emails, filling forms Multi-step task execution

These systems share three features: an open-ended action space (generating arbitrary natural language and code, not picking from fixed buttons), internal reasoning (planning before acting), and continuous interaction (adjusting strategy based on feedback).

The ReAct Loop: How Agents Actually Work

The core execution pattern is called ReAct (Reasoning + Acting). Despite the name mentioning only reasoning and acting, the actual loop has three stages: the model first reasons about what to do next, then calls a tool to act, then observes the tool’s result and reasons about the subsequent step.

Consider aggregating revenue across multiple currencies. The user asks: “Based on the company’s quarterly revenue: Q1 2.5M USD, Q2 2.1M EUR, Q3 1.8M GBP, Q4 380M JPY, calculate total annual revenue.”

The agent’s trajectory—the message history that accumulates as it works—looks like this:

A complex multi-step task was completed in 3 iterations and 4 tool calls. The elegance lies in the cumulative nature of the context: every LLM call receives the complete trajectory, so the model knows which stage it is in, what was tried before, and what the outcome was.

The key insight: Agent context = static prefix + trajectory. The static prefix (system prompt + tool definitions) stays fixed; the trajectory (user messages + assistant messages + tool results) grows with each interaction.

Context Engineering: The Ceiling of Agent Capability

Large language models achieve strong results on benchmarks, but often underperform in real-world settings. The reason is straightforward: model capabilities are general-purpose, while concrete tasks depend on local knowledge—product architecture, business rules, operational constraints. This information is absent from the model’s parameters.

Consider a Coding Agent given the instruction “Help me fix this bug.” The quality of the context it receives determines whether it can complete the task:

  • Code context: codebase structure, module responsibilities, coding standards. Without this, the agent may produce syntactically correct code that violates the project’s architecture.
  • Process requirements: Git branching strategy, commit conventions, CI/CD requirements. Without this, the agent may commit untested code directly to main.
  • Environment configuration: dev setup, test database connection strings, API key management. Without this, a fix that works locally fails in test.

The model’s inherent capability is only the foundation; context sets the ceiling. A moderately capable model with well-organized context can often outperform a stronger model operating with insufficient context.

Context at the API Level: Static Prefix + Dynamic Trajectory

At the API level, the context of each LLM call consists of five parts:

  • System Prompt: Developer-written instructions defining the agent’s identity, permissions, and rules of conduct. Stays fixed for the whole conversation.
  • Tool Definitions: Declares the names, descriptions, and parameter formats of available tools. Without them, the agent cannot recognize or call any tools.
  • User Messages: Input from the user, possibly containing external knowledge retrieved via RAG.
  • Assistant Messages: Previous model outputs, including reasoning, content, and tool_calls.
  • Tool Results: Output returned after the framework executes a tool.

The first two form the static prefix; the last three form the dynamic trajectory that grows with every interaction.

An ablation study reveals what happens when each component is removed:

Removed Component Effect on Agent
Tool Definitions Agent cannot recognize or call any tools—completely incapable of action
Tool Results Agent receives no execution feedback, calls the same tool repeatedly in an infinite loop
Reasoning in assistant messages Consecutive decisions start contradicting each other
Message history Agent loses task continuity, restarts from the beginning, repeats done steps

The core insight: context determines what information the agent has at decision time, and the agent can only decide based on that information.

KV Cache: Why Prefix Stability Matters

Every time the model generates a token, it refers back to intermediate computation results of preceding tokens. Recomputing those from scratch on every round would be expensive. KV Cache stores the key-value states so later computation can reuse them. The prerequisite: the prefix must stay completely unchanged.

A production incident illustrates the stakes. A team’s customer service agent handled 100,000 conversations a day. An engineer added a line Current time: {{now}} to the system prompt so the agent would know the current time. The next day, monitoring alerts fired: time-to-first-token increased from 0.5 seconds to 3–5 seconds, and the monthly inference bill nearly doubled.

That one timestamp line invalidated the KV Cache on every request. The system prompt was now different each time, forcing the model to recompute the key-value pairs for the prefix from scratch.

Three practical principles follow:

  1. Once the system prompt and tool definitions are finalized, do not change them. Any modification invalidates the entire cache.
  2. Always append dynamic information to the end. Timestamps and user status should be new messages at the end of the conversation, not modifications to the system prompt.
  3. Use the standard API format; do not manually concatenate messages. Structured messages are translated by the Chat Template into a fixed token sequence the model saw during training.

Prompt Engineering: Writing the Agent’s Operating Manual

A practical litmus test: an LLM is like a highly capable new team member who is completely unfamiliar with your specific workflows. If such a person, after reading your system prompt, still does not know what to do, neither will the agent.

Several dimensions matter:

Tone and style shape the user experience. Uppercase words like “NEVER do X” increase instruction salience, but overuse dilutes the effect—reserve them for truly critical constraints.

Structured prompts work because models are trained on structured data. XML tags carry semantic information (<working_directory> is immediately clear), and Markdown organizes content for both human and machine readers.

Process-driven prompts beat rule stacking. Imagine giving a new team member a manual with hundreds of scattered rules and no flowcharts. A process-driven prompt provides a clear Standard Operating Procedure:

Business rule refinement is the most critical—and most overlooked—piece. Vague rules like “choose the appropriate billing type based on the task situation” lead to unstable agent behavior. Rules must be defined to the point where they are executable: “NEVER use percentage-based billing for refunds. Use fixed_fee instead.”

An ablation study on prompt engineering found that removing structure from the system prompt (keeping all the rule content but converting the ordered process into an unstructured collection) dropped the task success rate by over 30%.

Agent Skills: Load Knowledge On Demand

As an agent handles more scenarios, the system prompt tends to grow: refund rules, coding standards, formatting requirements. Placing everything into a single prompt creates two problems: wasted tokens (most content is irrelevant to the current task) and diluted attention (irrelevant information drowns out key content).

Agent Skills solve this through Progressive Disclosure: instead of loading all knowledge at once, let the agent load knowledge on demand. Each Skill is a modular knowledge package with three layers:

  • Layer 1 (Metadata): A SKILL.md file with name and description fields, injected into context at startup. Usually only a few hundred tokens.
  • Layer 2 (Core Workflow): When the agent determines a skill is needed, it loads the full SKILL.md via a dedicated tool. The content appears as a tool result.
  • Layer 3 (Details): File references allow deeper navigation into sub-documents as needed.

The production implementation (used by Claude Code) injects the metadata list as a user-role meta message at the end of the context, wrapped in <system-reminder> tags. This does not modify the system prompt, so the KV Cache prefix remains stable. Full content is then loaded on demand via a dedicated tool.

Agent Status Bar: From Implicit State to Explicit Knowledge

The prompt engineering section solved “what static instructions to give the model.” But during execution, the agent also needs to track its own state dynamically. The Agent Status Bar addresses this.

The closest analogy is the status bar of an operating system. On a phone, the top of the screen displays time, battery level, and signal strength—giving users immediate access to device state. The Agent Status Bar serves a similar purpose for the model: it is a state summary injected at the end of the context.

Why is this needed? The theoretical basis is a fundamental property of attention: in-context learning is more retrieval-like than reasoning-like. The model is good at finding information that already exists in the context, but less reliable at actively summarizing and deriving aggregate state during a single forward pass.

Consider a phone-calling agent that must call each merchant no more than three times. After three calls, it often miscounts and makes a fourth. The problem: “How many times have I called?” is not automatically distilled into an explicit fact. It remains scattered across raw call records.

When we directly include the call count in each tool result:

The model can immediately recognize the limit is reached and stop. Experiments showed that for weak models, a precomputed status bar recovered accuracy by 40–54 percentage points; for strong models, it reduced reasoning tokens by 80–90% or more.

Three actionable lessons emerged:

  1. Maintain the status bar with code, not with an LLM. A 20-line regex function achieved ground-truth accuracy; a frontier model summarizing the full history produced many incorrect entries.
  2. Before deleting original context, confirm the status bar covers all questions. The status bar is a lossy projection. If a question asks for information it wasn’t designed to capture, accuracy can collapse.
  3. Monitor status bar accuracy as a first-line production metric. The model almost unconditionally trusts the status bar—if it says “called 3 times,” the model accepts that value without checking.

Context Compression: When Less Is More

As multi-turn interactions deepen, the context keeps expanding. Compression has two distinct motivations:

  1. Addressing length and cost constraints. The context window is limited, and a few rounds of tool calls can fill it.
  2. Improving reasoning quality. Summarized knowledge is more useful to the model than raw information.

The second motivation is deeper and easier to overlook. Suppose an agent accumulates information through 10 web searches. The raw results are scattered across tens of thousands of tokens. When the agent must make a final decision, its attention becomes diffuse.

After the 10th search, a single LLM call could produce a structured summary: “Currently known: A is…, B is…, information on C is still missing.” The model can then use this refined knowledge without re-extracting from raw data.

A phenomenon called Context Rot makes this critical. Context rot is different from context overflow: overflow means “cannot fit any more,” while rot means “it fits but cannot be found.” The agent appears to be working normally while decision quality quietly deteriorates.

Six compression strategies were compared in a research task (tracking OpenAI co-founders’ employment status):

Strategy Compression Ratio Tokens Iterations Notes
No Compression N/A overflow 5 Fails at 128K limit
Individual Summarization 10.9% 276,608 12 Information fragmentation
Combined Summarization 4.3% 93,449 10 May lose info at end
Context-Aware 3.0% 40,157 7 Best efficiency
Context-Aware + Citations 4.1% 222,992 — Verifiable
Adaptive Windowing varies 174,601 — Compresses only near limit

Context-aware compression—incorporating current query intent into the compression decision—reduced token usage by over 75% compared to naive approaches.

Production-grade systems like Claude Code use a hierarchical compression mechanism with five layers, applied in order of increasing cost:

  1. Tool result budget control: Large outputs stored on disk; model sees only a preview.
  2. Direct noise deletion: Low-value content removed without summarization.
  3. API-level micro-compression: Server removes specific tool results from prefix.
  4. Archival summarization: Structured round-by-round summarization (like git log).
  5. Full compression: LLM-driven complete compression, as a last resort with a circuit breaker.

What compression most easily loses is not the details themselves, but early architectural decisions, the reasoning behind constraints, and failed paths. Explicit retention priorities prevent this loss.

From Context to Memory: Making Agents Remember

The previous section addressed context management within a single session. But how do you enable an agent to remember users and retain knowledge even after a conversation ends?

This persistent memory system operates at two scales:

  • User Memory is personalized memory for an individual—the agent gradually learns each user’s preferences, habits, and needs.
  • Knowledge Base is collective knowledge shared across all users—industry regulations, company procedures, specialized documentation.

User Memory: Building a Model of the User

Memory is not a transcript of everything a user says. We don’t remember the raw content of every conversation with a friend; through repeated interaction we form a mental model of them.

After a conversation about booking a flight to Tokyo, the agent framework calls a dedicated LLM to extract information worth remembering:

Key characteristics: Selectivity (transient info is forgotten), Abstraction (specific instances become general preferences), and Structure (each memory is tagged with a type).

A three-level evaluation framework measures memory capabilities:

Level Capability Example
Level 1: Basic Recall Store and retrieve directly-provided info “My membership number is 12345”
Level 2: Multi-Session Retrieval Reason over info spanning different sessions User with two cars asks to “schedule maintenance”—agent finds both
Level 3: Proactive Service Synthesize across sessions to offer predictive help Booking international flight → surface expiring passport

Memory is divided into hierarchical levels, mirroring human cognition:

  • Trajectory: Complete history of a single session, append-only, never rewritten.
  • User Long-Term Memory: Persistent storage across sessions, repeatedly rewritten, merged, and pruned.

From a cognitive science perspective, long-term memory has three types, each with an agent counterpart:

Cognitive Type Human Example Agent Counterpart
Episodic Memory “Great dinner with colleagues last Wednesday” “User booked ANA flight to Tokyo next Friday”
Semantic Memory “Capital of Italy is Rome” “User is vegetarian, prefers window seats”
Procedural Memory Ability to ride a bicycle “First search direct flights → confirm seat → use FF number”

Four Storage Formats: From Simple Notes to Advanced JSON Cards

The same piece of user information can be represented with different granularities:

Simple Notes — Each memory is a minimal, indivisible fact (“User email: john@example.com“). Minimal overhead, but associations between facts are lost entirely. “Works as Senior Engineer at TechCorp on recommendation systems” becomes three disconnected fragments.

Enhanced Notes — Each memory is a paragraph with complete context. Preserves narrative structure, but suffers from storage redundancy, update complexity, and paragraphs too long for accurate retrieval.

JSON Cards — A three-level nested structure (Category → Subcategory → Key-Value), mimicking how humans categorize. Supports partial updates, but forces information into single categories.

Advanced JSON Cards — Each card records facts plus narrative context (backstory), subject identity (person), and relationship. Solves disambiguation: “Dr. Zhang” could be the user’s dentist or the user’s father’s cardiologist.

Format Strength Weakness
Simple Notes O(1) operations, minimal overhead Associations lost
Enhanced Notes Semantically complete Redundancy, hard to update
JSON Cards Structured, partial updates Forces single categorization
Advanced JSON Cards Disambiguation, rich context High maintenance cost

A hybrid approach works best in practice: Advanced JSON Cards for critical, low-volume data; Simple Notes for large volumes of non-critical facts.

RAG: Giving Agents a Knowledge Base

The core technology for building a shared knowledge base is Retrieval-Augmented Generation (RAG). The central idea: combine the LLM’s reasoning with the breadth and timeliness of an external knowledge base.

A typical RAG system has two parts: a retriever (finds relevant fragments) and a generator (uses fragments as context to generate an answer).

The quality of the retriever directly determines RAG’s effectiveness. Two main retrieval approaches complement each other:

Dense Embeddings map text into a vector space where semantically similar content has close vector distances. They understand that “kitty” and “cat” are related, but may miss exact keyword matches.

Sparse Embeddings (like BM25) are rooted in traditional keyword matching. A sparse vector has most dimensions zero—only dimensions for words in the document are non-zero. BM25 improves on TF-IDF by introducing term frequency saturation and document length normalization.

Hybrid retrieval combines both: run both engines in parallel, merge results using Reciprocal Rank Fusion (RRF), then apply a neural reranker for the final ordering.

Beyond Flat Text: Structured Indexing and Agentic RAG

Simple chunking has a fundamental limitation: it flattens knowledge, ignoring structure and cross-document relationships. Two cases illustrate this:

The Black Cat Counting Problem: If a knowledge base has 100 case documents (90 black cats, 10 white cats) and the user asks “What is the ratio?”, top-k retrieval returns only a sample. The model sees 15 black cats and 3 white cats and draws incorrect conclusions. A pre-generated summary (“Total: 90 black, 10 white”) solves this instantly.

The Xfinity Discount Problem: Three isolated cases—Veteran John got a discount, Doctor Sarah got a discount, Teacher Mike was ineligible. When a nurse inquires, the retriever prioritizes Sarah’s case (semantic similarity between “nurse” and “doctor”) and misses Mike’s case, leading to an incorrect inference that nurses are eligible.

Both cases point to the same conclusion: naive RAG is not enough. The model’s attention is a similarity-based soft retrieval system, not a thinking engine that actively summarizes. Compute must be invested at the indexing stage.

RAPTOR builds a tree hierarchy: cluster similar leaf nodes, generate parent summaries, and recurse upward. Retrieval can work at any abstraction level.

GraphRAG models knowledge as an entity-relationship graph. Its irreplaceable capability is multi-hop reasoning: “What is the address of my doctor’s hospital?” requires traversing user → doctor → hospital → address.

Method Structure Best For
RAPTOR Tree hierarchy Drilling down from concept to details
GraphRAG Entity-relationship graph “How does A relate to B?” queries

Agentic RAG turns retrieval from a fixed pipeline into a dynamic, iterative exploration. The knowledge base becomes a tool the agent calls at any time, following the ReAct loop:

Contextual Retrieval: Fixing Chunking at the Root

Even with agentic RAG, traditional chunking remains a bottleneck. An isolated fragment like “The company’s second-quarter revenue grew by 3%” is ambiguous—Which company? When? Which product line?

Contextual Retrieval fixes this at the source: before indexing, use an LLM to generate a short context prefix for each chunk, then concatenate it with the original text.

This strengthens both retrieval modes: BM25 gets rich matchable keywords (“ACME”, “2025 Q2”), and dense embeddings get accurate semantic background. According to Anthropic research, combining this with BM25 reduces the retrieval failure rate by 49%, and by 67% when combined with a reranker.

The Two-Tier Memory Architecture

The highest level of user memory—Proactive Service—demands both a global overview and precise details at once. Resident context alone loses details to capacity limits; retrieval alone misses hidden cross-session connections.

The solution is a two-tier memory architecture:

When the user books an international flight:

  1. Fact Review: Agent reviews JSON Cards, identifies “Tokyo trip” and “passport info”
  2. Association Reasoning: Flight date (January) is close to passport expiry (February)
  3. Detail Verification: Uses Contextual Retrieval to find original conversations about passport and flights
  4. Proactive Service: “Your passport is about to expire; I recommend expedited renewal.”

Harness Engineering: Reliability Beyond the Demo

The core formula describes the agent’s internal composition. But between a working demo and a reliable product lies a substantial gap. Harness Engineering is the implementation-level view: treat the LLM as one core component (the Model), and call all supporting code the Harness.

The expanded production-grade composition:

Agent = LLM + [Context + Tools + Constrain + Verify + Correct] = Model + Harness

A concrete example shows the value. Suppose you ask an agent to refund a user’s order placed 3 days ago:

Without Harness With Harness
No refund policy received (no context) System prompt specifies 7-day refund policy
Doesn’t know which API to call (no tools) Calls query_order and process_refund tools
Fabricates refund result (no verification) Framework checks refund doesn’t exceed order total
User discovers refund never happened (no correction) Confirms against database; auto-retries on timeout

Constrain, Verify, Correct: The Three Safety Layers

Function Core Principle Practical Example
Context Information Sufficiency System prompts, knowledge bases
Tools Clear Interface Tool names are intuitive, parameters have examples
Constrain Fail-Safe Defaults Every tool requires user authorization by default
Verify Input Isolation Security checks only look at structured data, not free-form text
Correct Hide intermediate states until failure confirmed Silent retries, circuit breaker on consecutive failures

Guardrails implement the constrain/verify/correct layer as defense in depth:

  • Input-side: Relevance classifiers, safety classifiers, content moderation, rule-based protections
  • Execution-side: Tool risk rating (low/medium/high), with high-risk operations requiring human confirmation
  • Output-side: PII filters, output validation against brand values

Workflow vs. Autonomous: Choosing the Right Pattern

Workflows orchestrate LLMs through predefined code paths. The execution path is deterministic—critical steps are never skipped. A flight-booking workflow has four fixed nodes: Verify Identity → Search Flights → Complete Payment → Confirm Booking. The system won’t book before payment is completed.

Autonomous Agents determine their execution path at runtime based on environmental feedback. The user says “Book me a flight to Shanghai next Wednesday” and the agent dynamically searches, verifies identity, adjusts criteria based on layovers, etc.

Pattern Advantage Limitation
Workflow Strict process control, security Lack of flexibility
Autonomous Agent Flexible, adapts to unexpected events Higher cost, errors compound

In practice, they are not mutually exclusive: critical processes with compliance requirements run as workflows, while flexible decisions switch to autonomous mode.

Three core principles for building effective agents:

  1. Keep it simple. Start with the simplest solution and add complexity only when necessary.
  2. Keep it transparent. Show the agent’s planning steps, execution logs, and decision trajectory.
  3. Design a well-structured tool interface (ACI). Tool names should be intuitive; the design should prevent likely mistakes (Poka-yoke).

Best Practices

Based on the concepts above, here are practical guidelines for building agents:

Context Design

  • Keep the system prompt and tool definitions stable once finalized—any change invalidates the KV Cache.
  • Append dynamic information (timestamps, status) at the end of the context, never in the system prompt.
  • Use structured formats (XML tags, Markdown) for instructions; provide process-driven SOPs, not scattered rules.
  • Define business rules to executable precision: “NEVER use percentage-based billing for refunds.”

Memory Design

  • Use a hybrid memory approach: Advanced JSON Cards for critical low-volume data, Simple Notes for large-volume non-critical facts.
  • Maintain the Agent Status Bar with code (regex functions), not with LLM summarization.
  • Monitor status bar accuracy as a first-line production metric—the model unconditionally trusts it.

Retrieval Design

  • Combine dense and sparse retrieval, then apply a neural reranker for production-grade RAG.
  • Apply Contextual Retrieval at the indexing phase—generate context prefixes for chunks before embedding.
  • Use Agentic RAG for complex questions requiring multi-hop reasoning; use simple RAG for clear, narrow queries.

Compression Design

  • Compress in batches when approaching the context limit, not every round.
  • Preserve architectural decisions, key constraints, verification status, and unresolved TODOs during compression.
  • Keep exact identifiers (UUIDs, hashes, URLs, filenames)—changing one digit breaks subsequent tool calls.

Safety Design

  • Tag external content with source markers to prevent prompt injection.
  • Implement tool risk ratings with human confirmation for high-risk operations.
  • Set failure thresholds and circuit breakers to prevent infinite loops.
  • Use sub-agent context isolation to keep bulky intermediate content out of the main context.

FAQ

Q: If models keep getting stronger, will context engineering still matter?

Directionally, models will internalize parts of the Harness—tool calling and long-horizon planning were once external orchestration and are now native capabilities. But in practice, this internalization is much slower than intuition suggests. Training takes months, and a model cannot internalize all constraints and preferences of real businesses in one pass. The model’s current capability boundary is exactly where the Harness creates value.

Q: What’s the difference between in-context learning and true memory?

In-context learning is fast but transient—it disappears when the session ends. Its mechanism is closer to pattern matching than true learning; it lets the model apply patterns it has already seen but cannot discover entirely new rules. User memory (persistent, reviewable storage) and externalized learning (knowledge bases, tool code) provide the reliability and longevity that in-context learning cannot.

Q: When should I use a workflow vs. an autonomous agent?

Start with a single LLM call. If better prompts solve the problem, don’t build an agent. When multiple steps are needed and the task decomposes into fixed sub-tasks, use a workflow. Use an autonomous agent only when you need dynamic decisions and a flexible execution path. Agent systems typically trade latency and cost for better task performance—evaluate whether that trade is worth it.

Q: How do I prevent prompt injection in my agent?

No single defense is sufficient—use layered defense. At the context level: tag external content with source markers (<external_content source="webpage">), use structured roles strictly, and sanitize suspicious patterns. At the execution level: implement tool risk ratings, require authorization for high-risk operations, and prevent retrieved content from directly triggering irreversible actions. Context-level defenses reduce the attack success rate but cannot guarantee complete security.

Q: Which retrieval strategy should I choose for my knowledge base?

If queries are primarily “find the document fragment containing this information,” hybrid retrieval (dense + sparse + reranking) is sufficient. If queries require cross-document synthesis or multi-level navigation, invest in structured indexing (RAPTOR or GraphRAG). Its cost is a large jump in LLM calls at index-construction time, so upgrade only when simpler options fall short.

Q: How often should I compress the context?

Compress in batches when the context approaches the threshold (e.g., 80% of window size), not every round. Frequent compression repeatedly breaks the cache. Use a hierarchical approach: tool result budget control first, then noise deletion, then API-level micro-compression, then archival summarization, and finally full compression as a last resort with a circuit breaker.

Summary

This article walked through the core ideas behind modern AI Agents along three layers:

The Core Formula: Agent = LLM + Context + Tools. The LLM provides reasoning, context supplies the working set of information at decision time, and tools provide action interfaces. The ReAct loop—reason, act, observe, repeat—connects them into a working system.

Context Engineering: Context sets the ceiling of agent capability. At the API level, context is a static prefix (system prompt + tool definitions) plus a dynamic trajectory (message history). KV Cache requires prefix stability. Prompt engineering writes the agent’s operating manual. Agent Skills load knowledge on demand. The Agent Status Bar converts implicit state into explicit knowledge. Context compression controls length and improves reasoning quality—not just by managing length, but by actively summarizing raw data into high-density structured knowledge.

From Context to Memory: User memory builds a model of the individual across sessions; the knowledge base provides shared domain expertise. Four storage formats trade off simplicity against expressiveness. RAG combines dense and sparse retrieval with neural reranking. Structured indexing (RAPTOR, GraphRAG) and Agentic RAG move beyond flat text. Contextual Retrieval fixes chunking at the root. The two-tier memory architecture—resident JSON Cards for overview, on-demand Contextual Retrieval for details—makes proactive service feasible.

Harness Engineering: Model capability is commoditizing; the real differentiator is the Harness—constrain, verify, and correct mechanisms built around context and tools. As models converge in capability, competitive advantage shifts to the engineering outside the model.

The common thread: do not let the model passively search through vast amounts of information; proactively provide refined, structured knowledge. This principle runs from prompt design through compression to the two-tier memory architecture—and it is the practice of the Bitter Lesson on an engineering timescale.

entry.title: 构建 AI Agent：从上下文到记忆
entry.content:
• 引言
  • 什么是 AI Agent
    • 核心公式：LLM + 上下文 + 工具
    • ReAct 循环：Agent 的实际运作方式
  • 上下文工程：Agent 能力的天花板
    • API 层面的上下文：静态前缀 + 动态轨迹
    • KV Cache：为什么前缀稳定性至关重要
    • 提示词工程：编写 Agent 的操作手册
    • Agent 技能：按需加载知识
    • Agent 状态栏：从隐式状态到显式知识
    • 上下文压缩：少即是多
  • 从上下文到记忆：让 Agent 拥有记忆力
    • 用户记忆：构建用户模型
    • 四种存储格式：从简单笔记到高级 JSON 卡片
    • RAG：为 Agent 赋予知识库
    • 超越扁平文本：结构化索引与 Agentic RAG
    • 上下文检索：从根源解决分块问题
    • 两层记忆架构
  • Harness 工程：超越 Demo 的可靠性
    • 约束、验证、纠正：三层安全保障
    • 工作流 vs. 自主模式：选择正确的模式
  • 最佳实践
  • 常见问题
  • 总结

引言

如果你用过 Cursor 写代码，看过它搜索代码库、编辑多个文件、反复运行测试直到通过，那你已经在使用 AI Agent 了。同样，如果你用 Deep Research 通过反复搜索和阅读来研究某个主题，或者让 Manus 控制浏览器完成在线任务，也是在使用 Agent。

这些产品形态各异，但有一个共同特征：它们不再是”你问它答”的被动对话。它们会自主规划执行步骤、调用每个任务所需的工具，并根据返回结果调整策略。

本文将从基础公式出发，依次讲解单次会话内的上下文工程，以及跨会话的持久记忆，梳理现代 AI Agent 的核心思想。目标是为你提供一套可用于构建自己 Agent 的心智模型。

什么是 AI Agent

核心公式：LLM + 上下文 + 工具

现代 Agent 系统的本质可以用一个简洁的公式概括：

Agent = LLM + 上下文 + 工具

每一项的含义都比表面看起来更广：

  • LLM 是推理引擎。 它是决策核心，负责理解意图、推理、规划和判断。其能力来自预训练阶段获得的世界知识，以及后训练阶段编码的决策策略。
  • 上下文是信息的 working set（工作集）。 不仅是输入模型的文本，而是在每个决策点可用的一切信息——环境状态、用户记忆、领域知识、Agent 自身状态以及任务进度。
  • 工具是 action interface（行动接口）。 Agent 可以采取行动的全部方式——从预定义的工具调用到按需加载的技能，从生成代码到将任务委派给子 Agent。

更直观地表达：Agent = 推理引擎 + 工作上下文 + 行动接口。模型负责推理和决策，上下文提供决策所依赖的信息，工具提供决策影响外部世界的接口。

不同类型的 Agent 在这三个维度上的对比：

Agent 产品 工作上下文 行动接口 策略
编程 Agent（Cursor） 需求、代码库、终端 代码搜索、文件读写、命令执行 理解 → 搜索 → 编辑 → 测试 → 调试
搜索 Agent（Deep Research） 网络资源、数据库 搜索查询、网页阅读、摘要生成 基于已有信息的迭代深入
电脑控制（Manus） 屏幕、浏览器、文件系统 点击、输入、滚动、截图 视觉感知 + 操作执行
手机助手（豆包） 手机屏幕、已安装应用 点击、滑动、打开应用 意图理解 + 应用控制
任务 Agent（Pine AI） 账户信息、历史账单 打电话、发邮件、填表单 多步骤任务执行

这些系统共享三个特征：开放式的行动空间（生成任意自然语言和代码，而非在固定按钮中选择）、内部推理（行动前先规划）、持续交互（根据反馈调整策略）。

ReAct 循环：Agent 的实际运作方式

核心执行模式称为 ReAct（Reasoning + Acting，推理 + 行动）。虽然名字只提到了推理和行动，但实际循环包含三个阶段：模型先推理下一步该做什么，然后调用工具行动，接着观察工具返回的结果并推理后续步骤。

考虑一个多币种收入汇总的场景。用户提问：”根据公司季度收入：Q1 250 万美元、Q2 210 万欧元、Q3 180 万英镑、Q4 3.8 亿日元，计算全年总收入。”

Agent 的轨迹（trajectory）——即工作过程中不断累积的消息历史——如下所示：

一个复杂的多步骤任务在 3 次迭代、4 次工具调用中完成。其优雅之处在于上下文的累积性：每次 LLM 调用都会接收完整的轨迹，因此模型知道当前处于哪个阶段、之前尝试过什么、结果如何。

关键洞察：Agent 上下文 = 静态前缀 + 轨迹。静态前缀（系统提示 + 工具定义）保持不变；轨迹（用户消息 + 助手消息 + 工具结果）随每次交互不断增长。

上下文工程：Agent 能力的天花板

大语言模型在基准测试中成绩优异，但在实际应用中往往表现不佳。原因很简单：模型能力是通用的，而具体任务依赖于本地知识——产品架构、业务规则、运维约束。这些信息不存在于模型参数中。

考虑一个收到”帮我修复这个 bug”指令的 Coding Agent。它收到的上下文质量决定了能否完成任务：

  • 代码上下文：代码库结构、模块职责、编码规范。缺少这些，Agent 可能生成语法正确但违反项目架构的代码。
  • 流程要求：Git 分支策略、提交规范、CI/CD 要求。缺少这些，Agent 可能直接将未经测试的代码提交到 main 分支。
  • 环境配置：开发环境设置、测试数据库连接字符串、API 密钥管理。缺少这些，在本地能跑的修复在测试环境中会失败。

模型的固有能力只是基础；上下文决定了天花板。一个能力中等但上下文组织良好的模型，往往能超越一个上下文不足的更强模型。

API 层面的上下文：静态前缀 + 动态轨迹

在 API 层面，每次 LLM 调用的上下文由五部分组成：

  • 系统提示（System Prompt）：开发者编写的指令，定义 Agent 的身份、权限和行为准则。在整个对话期间保持不变。
  • 工具定义（Tool Definitions）：声明可用工具的名称、描述和参数格式。没有它们，Agent 无法识别或调用任何工具。
  • 用户消息（User Messages）：来自用户的输入，可能包含通过 RAG 检索的外部知识。
  • 助手消息（Assistant Messages）：前次模型的输出，包括 reasoning、content 和 tool_calls。
  • 工具结果（Tool Results）：框架执行工具后返回的输出。

前两者构成静态前缀；后三者构成随每次交互增长的动态轨迹。

一项消融实验揭示了移除各组件后的影响：

被移除的组件 对 Agent 的影响
工具定义 Agent 无法识别或调用任何工具——完全丧失行动能力
工具结果 Agent 收不到执行反馈，反复调用同一工具，陷入无限循环
助手消息中的推理 连续决策之间开始相互矛盾
消息历史 Agent 丧失任务连续性，从头开始，重复已完成的步骤

核心洞察：上下文决定了 Agent 在决策时拥有哪些信息，而 Agent 只能基于这些信息做出决策。

KV Cache：为什么前缀稳定性至关重要

模型每生成一个 token，都需要参考前面 token 的中间计算结果。如果每轮都从头重新计算，开销会非常大。KV Cache 存储了键值状态，使后续计算可以复用它们。前提条件是：前缀必须完全不变。

一个生产事故说明了其重要性。某团队的客服 Agent 每天处理 10 万次对话。一位工程师在系统提示中加了一行 Current time: {{now}}，让 Agent 能知道当前时间。第二天，监控告警响起：首 token 延迟从 0.5 秒飙升到 3-5 秒，月度推理费用几乎翻倍。

那一行时间戳使每次请求的 KV Cache 都失效了。系统提示每次都不同，迫使模型从头重新计算前缀的键值对。

由此得出三条实用原则：

  1. 系统提示和工具定义一旦确定，就不要修改。 任何改动都会使整个缓存失效。
  2. 始终将动态信息追加到末尾。 时间戳和用户状态应该作为对话末尾的新消息，而非修改系统提示。
  3. 使用标准 API 格式，不要手动拼接消息。 结构化消息由 Chat Template 转换为模型训练时见过的固定 token 序列。

提示词工程：编写 Agent 的操作手册

一个实用的试金石：LLM 就像一个能力很强但完全不了解你具体工作流程的新团队成员。如果这样一个人读完你的系统提示后仍然不知道该做什么，Agent 也一样。

几个重要的维度：

语气和风格塑造用户体验。像”NEVER do X”这样的大写词能提高指令的显著性，但过度使用会削弱效果——留给真正关键的约束。

结构化提示之所以有效，是因为模型是在结构化数据上训练的。XML 标签携带语义信息（<working_directory> 一目了然），Markdown 同时为人类和机器组织内容。

流程驱动的提示优于规则堆砌。想象给新团队成员一本手册，里面散落着数百条规则，却没有流程图。流程驱动的提示提供清晰的标准操作流程（SOP）：

业务规则的细化是最关键也最容易被忽视的部分。像”根据任务情况选择合适的计费类型”这样模糊的规则会导致 Agent 行为不稳定。规则必须定义到可执行的程度：”NEVER use percentage-based billing for refunds. Use fixed_fee instead.”

一项关于提示词工程的消融实验发现，移除系统提示中的结构（保留所有规则内容，但将有序流程转换为无结构的集合）会使任务成功率下降超过 30%。

Agent 技能：按需加载知识

随着 Agent 处理的场景越来越多，系统提示会不断膨胀：退款规则、编码规范、格式要求。将所有内容放在一个提示中会产生两个问题：token 浪费（大部分内容与当前任务无关）和注意力稀释（无关信息淹没了关键内容）。

Agent 技能（Skills）通过渐进式披露（Progressive Disclosure）来解决这个问题：不是一次性加载所有知识，而是让 Agent 按需加载。每个技能是一个模块化的知识包，分为三层：

  • 第一层（元数据）：一个 SKILL.md 文件，包含 name 和 description 字段，在启动时注入上下文。通常只有几百个 token。
  • 第二层（核心工作流）：当 Agent 判断需要某个技能时，通过专用工具加载完整的 SKILL.md。内容以工具结果的形式出现。
  • 第三层（细节）：文件引用允许按需深入查阅子文档。

生产环境的实现（Claude Code 使用的方式）将元数据列表作为 user 角色的 meta 消息注入到上下文末尾，用 <system-reminder> 标签包裹。这样不修改系统提示，KV Cache 前缀保持稳定。完整内容随后通过专用工具按需加载。

Agent 状态栏：从隐式状态到显式知识

提示词工程部分解决了”给模型什么静态指令”的问题。但在执行过程中，Agent 还需要动态跟踪自身状态。Agent 状态栏正是为此而生。

最贴切的类比是操作系统的状态栏。在手机上，屏幕顶部显示时间、电量和信号强度——让用户即时了解设备状态。Agent 状态栏对模型的作用类似：它是注入到上下文末尾的状态摘要。

为什么需要这个？理论基础是注意力的一个基本特性：上下文内学习（in-context learning）更像检索而非推理。模型擅长在上下文中找到已存在的信息，但在单次前向传播中主动总结和推导聚合状态时不太可靠。

考虑一个打电话的 Agent，要求对每个商家最多拨打三次电话。三次之后，它经常数错并拨打第四次。问题在于：”我打了多少次电话？”并没有自动提炼为一个明确的事实，而是分散在原始的通话记录中。

当我们在每次工具结果中直接包含通话计数：

模型可以立即识别到已达到上限并停止。实验表明，对于弱模型，预计算的状态栏可将准确率恢复 40-54 个百分点；对于强模型，可减少 80-90% 甚至更多的推理 token。

三条可操作的经验：

  1. 用代码维护状态栏，而非 LLM。 一个 20 行的正则函数就能达到真实值的准确率；而前沿模型总结全部历史却产生大量错误条目。
  2. 在删除原始上下文之前，确认状态栏覆盖了所有问题。 状态栏是有损投影。如果问题涉及它未被设计捕获的信息，准确率会崩塌。
  3. 将状态栏准确率作为一线生产指标监控。 模型几乎无条件信任状态栏——如果它说”已拨打 3 次”，模型会不加验证地接受这个值。

上下文压缩：少即是多

随着多轮交互的深入，上下文不断膨胀。压缩有两个不同的动机：

  1. 应对长度和成本约束。 上下文窗口有限，几轮工具调用就可能将其填满。
  2. 提升推理质量。 经过提炼的知识比原始信息对模型更有用。

第二个动机更深层也更容易被忽视。假设一个 Agent 通过 10 次网络搜索积累信息，原始结果分散在数万个 token 中。当 Agent 需要做最终决策时，其注意力变得分散。

在第 10 次搜索后，一次 LLM 调用就可以生成结构化摘要：”当前已知：A 是……，B 是……，C 的信息仍然缺失。”模型随后可以使用这些提炼后的知识，而无需从原始数据中重新提取。

一种称为上下文腐烂（Context Rot）的现象使这一点至关重要。上下文腐烂不同于上下文溢出：溢出是”放不下了”，而腐烂是”放得下但找不到”。Agent 看起来在正常工作，但决策质量在悄然下降。

一项研究任务（追踪 OpenAI 联合创始人的在职状态）比较了六种压缩策略：

策略 压缩比 Token 数 迭代次数 备注
不压缩 不适用 溢出 5 在 128K 限制处失败
逐条摘要 10.9% 276,608 12 信息碎片化
合并摘要 4.3% 93,449 10 末尾可能丢失信息
上下文感知 3.0% 40,157 7 最佳效率
上下文感知 + 引用 4.1% 222,992 — 可验证
自适应窗口 可变 174,601 — 仅在接近限制时压缩

上下文感知压缩——将当前查询意图纳入压缩决策——相比朴素方法减少了超过 75% 的 token 使用量。

Claude Code 等生产级系统使用分层压缩机制，包含五个层级，按成本递增顺序应用：

  1. 工具结果预算控制：大输出存储到磁盘，模型只看到预览。
  2. 直接删除噪声：低价值内容直接移除，不做摘要。
  3. API 级微压缩：服务端从前缀中移除特定工具结果。
  4. 归档摘要：结构化的逐轮摘要（类似 git log）。
  5. 全量压缩：LLM 驱动的完整压缩，作为带有断路器的最后手段。

压缩最容易丢失的不是细节本身，而是早期的架构决策、约束背后的理由以及失败的路径。显式的保留优先级可以防止这种损失。

从上下文到记忆：让 Agent 拥有记忆力

前面的章节讨论了单次会话内的上下文管理。但如何让 Agent 在对话结束后仍然记住用户、保留知识？

这个持久记忆系统在两个尺度上运作：

  • 用户记忆（User Memory） 是针对个人的个性化记忆——Agent 逐渐学习每个用户的偏好、习惯和需求。
  • 知识库（Knowledge Base） 是所有用户共享的集体知识——行业法规、公司流程、专业文档。

用户记忆：构建用户模型

记忆不是用户说过的所有话的逐字记录。我们不会记住与朋友每次对话的原始内容；通过反复互动，我们形成了关于对方的心智模型。

在一次关于预订飞往东京航班的对话后，Agent 框架调用一个专用 LLM 来提取值得记住的信息：

关键特征：选择性（短暂的信息被遗忘）、抽象性（具体事例变成一般偏好）、结构性（每条记忆都标有类型）。

一个三级评估框架衡量记忆能力：

级别 能力 示例
第一级：基础回忆 存储和检索直接提供的信息 “我的会员号是 12345”
第二级：跨会话检索 对跨越不同会话的信息进行推理 有两辆车的用户要求”安排保养”——Agent 找到两辆
第三级：主动服务 跨会话综合信息提供预测性帮助 预订国际航班 → 提示护照即将过期

记忆被划分为层次化级别，对应人类认知：

  • 轨迹（Trajectory）：单次会话的完整历史，只追加，不重写。
  • 用户长期记忆：跨会话的持久存储，反复重写、合并和修剪。

从认知科学的角度，长期记忆有三种类型，每种都有 Agent 对应物：

认知类型 人类示例 Agent 对应物
情景记忆 “上周三和同事吃了顿很棒的晚餐” “用户预订了下周五飞往东京的 ANA 航班”
语义记忆 “意大利的首都是罗马” “用户是素食主义者，偏好靠窗座位”
程序性记忆 骑自行车的能力 “先搜直飞 → 确认座位 → 使用常旅客号码”

四种存储格式：从简单笔记到高级 JSON 卡片

同一条用户信息可以用不同粒度来表示：

简单笔记（Simple Notes） —— 每条记忆是一个最小的、不可再分的事实（”User email: john@example.com“）。开销最小，但事实之间的关联完全丢失。”在 TechCorp 担任高级工程师，做推荐系统”变成三个不相连的碎片。

增强笔记（Enhanced Notes） —— 每条记忆是一个包含完整上下文的段落。保留了叙事结构，但存在存储冗余、更新复杂度高、段落过长影响检索准确性等问题。

JSON 卡片（JSON Cards） —— 三级嵌套结构（类别 → 子类别 → 键值对），模拟人类的分类方式。支持部分更新，但强制信息归入单一类别。

高级 JSON 卡片（Advanced JSON Cards） —— 每张卡片记录事实 + 叙事背景（backstory）、主体身份（person）和关系。解决歧义问题：”张医生”可能是用户的牙医，也可能是用户父亲的心脏科医生。

格式 优势 劣势
简单笔记 O(1) 操作，开销最小 关联丢失
增强笔记 语义完整 冗余，难以更新
JSON 卡片 结构化，支持部分更新 强制单一分类
高级 JSON 卡片 消歧，丰富的上下文 维护成本高

实践中混合使用效果最好：对关键的、少量的的数据使用高级 JSON 卡片；对大量的、非关键的事实使用简单笔记。

RAG：为 Agent 赋予知识库

构建共享知识库的核心技术是检索增强生成（Retrieval-Augmented Generation，RAG）。核心思想：将 LLM 的推理能力与外部知识库的广度和时效性相结合。

一个典型的 RAG 系统有两部分：检索器（找到相关片段）和生成器（将片段作为上下文生成答案）。

检索器的质量直接决定了 RAG 的效果。两种主要的检索方法互为补充：

稠密嵌入（Dense Embeddings） 将文本映射到向量空间，语义相似的内容向量距离相近。它们能理解”kitty”和”cat”是相关的，但可能错过精确的关键词匹配。

稀疏嵌入（Sparse Embeddings）（如 BM25）源自传统的关键词匹配。稀疏向量的大部分维度为零——只有文档中出现的词对应的维度非零。BM25 在 TF-IDF 的基础上引入了词频饱和和文档长度归一化。

混合检索将两者结合：并行运行两个引擎，使用倒数排名融合（Reciprocal Rank Fusion，RRF）合并结果，再用神经重排序器（reranker）做最终排序。

超越扁平文本：结构化索引与 Agentic RAG

简单的分块有一个根本性的局限：它将知识扁平化，忽略了结构和跨文档关系。两个案例说明了这一点：

黑猫计数问题：如果知识库有 100 个案例文档（90 只黑猫，10 只白猫），用户问”比例是多少？”，top-k 检索只返回一个样本。模型看到 15 只黑猫和 3 只白猫，得出了错误的结论。一个预生成的摘要（”总计：90 只黑猫，10 只白猫”）就能立即解决。

Xfinity 折扣问题：三个孤立的案例——退伍军人 John 获得了折扣，医生 Sarah 获得了折扣，教师 Mike 不符合资格。当一位护士咨询时，检索器优先返回 Sarah 的案例（”nurse”和”doctor”的语义相似度），遗漏了 Mike 的案例，导致错误推断护士也有资格。

两个案例指向同一个结论：朴素的 RAG 不够用。模型的注意力是基于相似度的软检索系统，而不是主动总结的思考引擎。必须在索引阶段投入计算。

RAPTOR 构建树形层次结构：对相似的叶节点聚类，生成父级摘要，递归向上。检索可以在任何抽象层级进行。

GraphRAG 将知识建模为实体-关系图。其不可替代的能力是多跳推理：”我的医生所在医院的地址是什么？”需要遍历 用户 → 医生 → 医院 → 地址。

方法 结构 最适用场景
RAPTOR 树形层次结构 从概念下钻到细节
GraphRAG 实体-关系图 “A 和 B 的关系是什么？”类查询

Agentic RAG 将检索从固定管道变为动态的、迭代式的探索。知识库成为 Agent 随时可调用的工具，遵循 ReAct 循环：

上下文检索：从根源解决分块问题

即使有了 Agentic RAG，传统的分块仍然是瓶颈。一个孤立的片段如”公司第二季度收入增长了 3%”是模糊的——哪家公司？什么时候？哪条产品线？

上下文检索（Contextual Retrieval） 从源头修复这个问题：在索引之前，用 LLM 为每个分块生成一个简短的上下文前缀，然后将其与原始文本拼接。

这同时增强了两种检索模式：BM25 获得了丰富的可匹配关键词（”ACME”、”2025 Q2”），稠密嵌入获得了准确的语义背景。根据 Anthropic 的研究，与 BM25 结合时检索失败率降低 49%，加上 reranker 后降低 67%。

两层记忆架构

用户记忆的最高层次——主动服务——需要同时具备全局概览和精确细节。仅靠常驻上下文会因容量限制丢失细节；仅靠检索会遗漏隐含的跨会话关联。

解决方案是两层记忆架构：

当用户预订国际航班时：

  1. 事实回顾：Agent 回顾 JSON Cards，识别出”东京行程”和”护照信息”
  2. 关联推理：航班日期（一月）接近护照到期日（二月）
  3. 细节验证：使用上下文检索查找关于护照和航班的原始对话
  4. 主动服务：”您的护照即将到期，建议尽快办理加急换发。”

Harness 工程：超越 Demo 的可靠性

核心公式描述了 Agent 的内部组成。但在可运行的 Demo 和可靠的产品之间存在巨大差距。Harness 工程是实施层面的视角：将 LLM 视为一个核心组件（Model），将所有辅助代码称为 Harness。

扩展后的生产级组成：

Agent = LLM + [Context + Tools + Constrain + Verify + Correct] = Model + Harness

一个具体例子展示了其价值。假设你让 Agent 为一笔 3 天前的订单退款：

没有 Harness 有 Harness
未收到退款策略（无上下文） 系统提示指定 7 天退款政策
不知道该调用哪个 API（无工具） 调用 query_order 和 process_refund 工具
捏造退款结果（无验证） 框架检查退款金额不超过订单总额
用户发现退款从未执行（无纠正） 与数据库确认；超时自动重试

约束、验证、纠正：三层安全保障

功能 核心原则 实践示例
上下文 信息充分性 系统提示、知识库
工具 清晰的接口 工具名称直观，参数有示例
约束 故障安全默认值 每个工具默认需要用户授权
验证 输入隔离 安全检查只看结构化数据，不看自由文本
纠正 在确认失败之前隐藏中间状态 静默重试，连续失败时触发断路器

护栏（Guardrails）以纵深防御的方式实现约束/验证/纠正层：

  • 输入侧：相关性分类器、安全分类器、内容审核、基于规则的防护
  • 执行侧：工具风险评级（低/中/高），高风险操作需要人工确认
  • 输出侧：PII 过滤器、输出值与品牌价值的校验

工作流 vs. 自主模式：选择正确的模式

工作流（Workflows） 通过预定义的代码路径编排 LLM。执行路径是确定性的——关键步骤不会被跳过。一个航班预订工作流有四个固定节点：验证身份 → 搜索航班 → 完成支付 → 确认预订。系统不会在支付完成前就预订。

自主 Agent（Autonomous Agents） 在运行时根据环境反馈确定执行路径。用户说”帮我订一张下周三飞上海的机票”，Agent 动态地搜索、验证身份、根据中转情况调整条件等。

模式 优势 局限
工作流 严格的流程控制，安全性 缺乏灵活性
自主 Agent 灵活，能适应意外情况 成本更高，错误会累积

实践中，二者并非互斥：有合规要求的关键流程用工作流，灵活的决策切换为自主模式。

构建高效 Agent 的三个核心原则：

  1. 保持简单。 从最简方案开始，只在必要时增加复杂度。
  2. 保持透明。 展示 Agent 的规划步骤、执行日志和决策轨迹。
  3. 设计结构良好的工具接口（ACI）。 工具名称应直观易懂；设计应防止可能的误操作（防呆设计/Poka-yoke）。

最佳实践

基于上述概念，以下是构建 Agent 的实践指南：

上下文设计

  • 系统提示和工具定义一旦确定就保持稳定——任何改动都会使 KV Cache 失效。
  • 将动态信息（时间戳、状态）追加在上下文末尾，永远不要放在系统提示中。
  • 使用结构化格式（XML 标签、Markdown）编写指令；提供流程驱动的 SOP，而非散落的规则。
  • 将业务规则定义到可执行的精度：”NEVER use percentage-based billing for refunds.”

记忆设计

  • 采用混合记忆方案：关键少量数据用高级 JSON 卡片，大量非关键事实用简单笔记。
  • 用代码（正则函数）维护 Agent 状态栏，而非 LLM 摘要。
  • 将状态栏准确率作为一线生产指标监控——模型无条件信任它。

检索设计

  • 结合稠密检索和稀疏检索，再用神经重排序器，构建生产级 RAG。
  • 在索引阶段应用上下文检索——在嵌入之前为分块生成上下文前缀。
  • 对需要多跳推理的复杂问题使用 Agentic RAG；对明确、窄范围的查询使用简单 RAG。

压缩设计

  • 在接近上下文限制时按批次压缩，而非每轮都压缩。
  • 压缩时保留架构决策、关键约束、验证状态和未完成的 TODO。
  • 保留精确的标识符（UUID、哈希、URL、文件名）——改一个数字就会导致后续工具调用失败。

安全设计

  • 用来源标记标注外部内容，防止提示注入。
  • 实施工具风险评级，高风险操作需要人工确认。
  • 设置失败阈值和断路器，防止无限循环。
  • 使用子 Agent 上下文隔离，将大量中间内容排除在主上下文之外。

常见问题

Q：如果模型越来越强，上下文工程还重要吗？

方向上，模型会内化 Harness 的部分能力——工具调用和长期规划曾经是外部编排的功能，现在已是原生能力。但实际上，这种内化比直觉上认为的要慢得多。训练需要数月时间，模型不可能一次性内化所有真实业务的约束和偏好。模型当前的能力边界，恰恰是 Harness 创造价值的地方。

Q：上下文内学习和真正的记忆有什么区别？

上下文内学习快速但短暂——会话结束就消失了。其机制更接近模式匹配而非真正的学习；它让模型应用已经见过的模式，但无法发现全新的规则。用户记忆（持久、可审查的存储）和外化学习（知识库、工具代码）提供了上下文内学习无法提供的可靠性和持久性。

Q：什么时候用工作流，什么时候用自主 Agent？

从单次 LLM 调用开始。如果更好的提示就能解决问题，就不要构建 Agent。当需要多个步骤且任务可分解为固定子任务时，使用工作流。只有在需要动态决策和灵活执行路径时才使用自主 Agent。Agent 系统通常以延迟和成本换取更好的任务表现——评估这个权衡是否值得。

Q：如何防止 Agent 中的提示注入？

单一防御不够——需要纵深防御。在上下文层面：用来源标记标注外部内容（<external_content source="webpage">），严格使用结构化角色，过滤可疑模式。在执行层面：实施工具风险评级，高风险操作需要授权，防止检索到的内容直接触发不可逆操作。上下文层防御可以降低攻击成功率，但不能保证完全安全。

Q：知识库应该选择哪种检索策略？

如果查询主要是”找到包含这个信息的文档片段”，混合检索（稠密 + 稀疏 + 重排序）就足够了。如果查询需要跨文档综合或多层导航，投资结构化索引（RAPTOR 或 GraphRAG）。其成本是索引构建时 LLM 调用量的大幅跃升，因此只在简单方案不够用时再升级。

Q：应该多频繁地压缩上下文？

在上下文接近阈值（例如窗口大小的 80%）时按批次压缩，而非每轮都压缩。频繁压缩会反复破坏缓存。采用分层方法：先工具结果预算控制，再噪声删除，再 API 级微压缩，再归档摘要，最后全量压缩作为带有断路器的最后手段。

总结

本文沿着三个层次梳理了现代 AI Agent 的核心思想：

核心公式：Agent = LLM + 上下文 + 工具。LLM 提供推理，上下文提供决策时的信息工作集，工具提供行动接口。ReAct 循环——推理、行动、观察、重复——将它们连接成一个可运作的系统。

上下文工程：上下文决定了 Agent 能力的天花板。在 API 层面，上下文是静态前缀（系统提示 + 工具定义）加上动态轨迹（消息历史）。KV Cache 要求前缀稳定。提示词工程编写 Agent 的操作手册。Agent 技能按需加载知识。Agent 状态栏将隐式状态转化为显式知识。上下文压缩控制长度并提升推理质量——不仅是管理长度，更是主动将原始数据提炼为高密度的结构化知识。

从上下文到记忆：用户记忆在跨会话中构建个人模型；知识库提供共享的领域专业知识。四种存储格式在简洁性和表达力之间权衡。RAG 将稠密检索和稀疏检索与神经重排序相结合。结构化索引（RAPTOR、GraphRAG）和 Agentic RAG 超越了扁平文本。上下文检索从根源修复分块问题。两层记忆架构——常驻 JSON Cards 提供概览，按需上下文检索提供细节——使主动服务成为可能。

Harness 工程：模型能力正在商品化；真正的差异化在于 Harness——围绕上下文和工具构建的约束、验证和纠正机制。随着模型能力趋同，竞争优势转向模型之外的工程。

贯穿始终的主线：不要让模型被动地在海量信息中搜索；主动提供经过提炼的、结构化的知识。 这一原则从提示设计贯穿到压缩再到两层记忆架构——它也是 Bitter Lesson（苦涩的教训）在工程时间尺度上的实践。

entry.title: 搭建属于你自己的AI技能
entry.content:
• 引言
  • 什么是技能（Skill）
  • 为什么技能很重要
  • 技能的解剖结构
    • SKILL.md 文件
    • 配角阵容
  • 动手搭建：从简单到完整
    • Git 提交信息：只要一个 SKILL.md
    • API 端点生成器：加一份配置
    • React 组件生成器：脚本与模板
    • 安全审计：参考文档
    • 你需要哪种结构？
  • 寻找现成的技能
    • 官方技能库
    • Skills CLI
    • 社区技能库
    • 安装前的安全检查
  • 将技能融入你的工作流
  • 迭代与版本管理
  • 最佳实践
  • 常见问题
  • 总结

引言

这周你已经把同一个提示词敲了三遍。每一次，AI 给你的回答都略有不同——周一它用 Tab 缩进，今天它用空格，中间某次它还悄悄”优化”了一个你根本没让它碰的函数。

这就是**”吩咐”与“教会”**之间的区别。

当你和 AI 对话时，你给的是一条口头指令，模型每次都要重新解读一遍。而当你写下一个技能（Skill）时，你交给它的是一本成文的操作手册——一份标准作业程序（SOP），它可以每次都一字不差地照着执行，在每个项目里都保持一致。

如果提示词是一句口头命令，那么技能就是打印出来的 SOP。

这篇文章会告诉你：技能是什么、为什么重要，以及最重要的——如何搭建属于你自己的技能。读完之后，你将掌握一套可复用的方法，把那些”我又在敲同一个提示词”的时刻，变成你个人的 AI 工具箱。

什么是技能（Skill）

技能是一组可复用的指令，它把某项特定能力打包起来。

想想做菜。每次凭记忆烧一道菜，你都可能漏掉某种配料或某个步骤。但如果把菜谱写下来一次，你就能每次都完美复刻——还能把它分享给别人。技能就是这样一份菜谱，只不过是写给 AI 的。

它与一次性提示词的对比正是全部意义所在：

维度 单个提示词 技能
本质 一次性指令 可复用的标准流程
一致性 每次输出都不一样 每次都遵循同一标准
成本 每次都要重新写 触发一次即可
维护 用完即弃 可版本化、可持续改进
类比 一句口头命令 一份成文的 SOP（标准作业程序）

技能不是一种新模型，也不是运行在 AI”外部”的插件。它只是指令加资源，按照一定的结构组织起来，让 AI 能在需要时精准加载所需内容。正是这种简单性让它行之有效。

为什么技能很重要

四个实实在在的好处，按它们真正为你节省的程度排序：

  1. 一致性 —— AI 每次都遵循同一标准。再也不用忍受”今天 Tab、明天空格”。
  2. 效率 —— 复杂的多步骤工作流收缩成一次触发，而不是一段反复重写的提示词。
  3. 可复用性 —— 一个技能可以跨项目、跨团队使用，最佳实践不再只存在于你的脑子里。
  4. 可迭代性 —— 技能是一个你可以持续改进的文件，所以它会越用_越好_，而不是原地冻结。

这里有一个你早就熟悉的编程原则：DRY —— Don’t Repeat Yourself（不要重复自己）。 它不仅适用于代码，也适用于提示词。如果类似的提示词你已经写了三遍，那就该把它变成技能了。

技能之所以重要的更深层原因是：大模型的训练数据里不可能内置每个领域的最佳实践。技能是你按需注入_你的_专业知识的方式——你团队的约定、你的安全标准、你的模板。这就是”聪明的通才”与_你的_领域专家之间的区别。

技能的解剖结构

先说一个人们最常搞错的点：技能是一个文件夹，而不是一个文件。 单个 Markdown 文件可能就够用了，但一个完整的技能是一个小型”能力包”，可能捆绑多种类型的文件。

继续用菜谱来类比：

  • SKILL.md 是菜谱本身——菜名、步骤、注意事项。
  • scripts/ 是厨房工具抽屉——处理琐碎工作的辅助脚本。
  • resources/ 是配料包——模板、示例数据和配置。
  • references/ 是后墙的参考书架——AI 可以查阅的标准和文档。
  • requirements.txt 声明脚本需要哪些第三方依赖包。

标准的目录结构长这样：

只有 SKILL.md 是必需的。其他一切都是可选的，只有在确实需要时才添加。

SKILL.md 文件

SKILL.md 是技能的心脏。它由两部分组成：一个可选的 frontmatter（元数据）块，以及承载实际指令的正文。

frontmatter 是可选的——很多技能干脆不写它。但当一个技能需要被智能体系统_自动发现_时，trigger 和 description 字段就变得重要了。智能体在启动时只读取元数据，只有当任务匹配时才加载完整指令。这种渐进式披露（progressive disclosure）设计节省了上下文窗口的空间，这在长会话中至关重要。

配角阵容

四个可选目录各自解决不同的问题：

scripts/ —— 辅助脚本。 当技能需要真正的逻辑（数据清洗、批量文件操作、格式校验）时，把它移进脚本可以让 SKILL.md 保持干净。AI 只需调用脚本，而不用重新推导逻辑。

resources/ —— 生产物料。 模板、示例和配置文件。它们被_直接使用_来产出结果：

  • template/ —— AI 生成输出所依据的代码/文档模板。
  • examples/ —— 输入/输出示例对，展示”好的输出长什么样”。
  • config/ —— 存放规则和默认值的 JSON/YAML 文件，避免把它们硬编码进 SKILL.md。

references/ —— 参考书架。 与 resources/ 不同，这些内容_不会_被复制进输出；它们是 AI 为了做出正确决策而阅读的知识。编码规范、安全检查清单（如 OWASP Top 10）、API 文档和技术决策记录都属于这里。

一句话区分 resources/ 与 references/： resources/ 是你用来构建的_物料_（模板、配置）；references/ 是你用来查阅的_手册_（标准、规则）。

requirements.txt —— 依赖声明。 如果 scripts/ 用到了第三方库，把它们列在这里，环境就能一步搭建完成。

动手搭建：从简单到完整

现在到了你期待已久的部分。搭建技能最重要的一条规则：

用能解决问题的最简单结构。

不是每个技能都需要每个目录。下面四个示例从单文件一路演进到完整能力包，每个示例教会你结构中的一个组成部分。读完之后，你就会清楚_你的_技能到底需要多少结构。

Git 提交信息：只要一个 SKILL.md

目标： 每次都不假思索地生成一条 Conventional Commits 格式的提交信息。

这是最简单的技能——只有一个 SKILL.md，别无其他。

创建 .claude/skills/git-commit/SKILL.md：

就这样。没有脚本，没有模板——而它能用，因为这项工作纯粹是遵循指令。一旦你的任务需要真正的逻辑或固定的输出格式，就要添加目录了，如下面的示例所示。

API 端点生成器：加一份配置

目标： 生成标准的 CRUD 端点，全部返回相同的 JSON 结构。

这个技能新增了一个组成部分：resources/config/。它把响应格式存放在文件里，而不是硬编码在指令中。

创建 SKILL.md：

以及配置文件 .claude/skills/api-endpoint/resources/config/response-format.json：

这里的好处是关注点分离：只需编辑一个 JSON 文件就能改变响应结构，完全不用碰指令。SKILL.md 保持简短，格式在所有使用处保持一致。

React 组件生成器：脚本与模板

目标： 每个新 React 组件都遵循相同的文件结构、编码风格和测试配置。

这是一个_完整的_技能包——它用 scripts/ 做校验，用 resources/template/ 保证代码一致性。

先搭好目录结构：

SKILL.md 定义了完整契约：

校验脚本 scripts/validate.js 给技能内置了一个自检机制：

模板 resources/template/component.tsx.tpl 给 AI 提供了一个具体的参考形态（不是让它逐字照抄，而是一种要遵循的_风格_）：

为什么模板胜过纯文字描述。 “干净、带类型、函数式组件”这样的文字描述是含糊的；而模板向 AI 精确展示了你的意思。它产出的质量永远高于一段文字描述。

配置好之后，你只需要一句话就能使用它：

安全审计：参考文档

目标： 按照_你的_标准审计代码，而不是靠 AI 的泛泛猜测。

前面三个示例覆盖了 scripts/、resources/ 和一个裸 SKILL.md。这一个则重点介绍 **references/**——当 AI 必须依据特定的外部规则行事时，这个目录就至关重要。

SKILL.md 告诉 AI _该做什么、规则在哪里_：

参考文档是你团队_具体_要求存放的地方——那些通用模型永远不可能知道的内容：

为什么 references/ 值得投入。 没有它，AI 只会用它的_通用_知识做审计，漏掉你团队的_具体_规则。有了它，审计标准就变得确定、可控、可迭代——规则变了就更新 references/team-security-standards.md，之后每一次审计都会立刻遵循新规则。

你需要哪种结构？

把四个示例并排放在一起，结论就显而易见了：

示例 核心组成部分 它教会你什么
Git 提交 仅 SKILL.md 最简单的技能形态
API 端点 SKILL.md + resources/config/ 配置外部化
React 组件 SKILL.md + scripts/ + resources/template/ 脚本校验 + 模板
安全审计 SKILL.md + references/ + resources/examples/ 参考文档驱动的审查

这里有一份为你自己的技能准备的快速决策指南：

场景 推荐结构
编码规范 仅 SKILL.md
代码生成 SKILL.md + resources/template/
数据处理 SKILL.md + scripts/ + resources/config/
质量审查 SKILL.md + references/
完整工程化流程 以上全部

寻找现成的技能

你不必从零开始。一个成熟的技能生态已经存在，高效的路径是寻找 → 评估 → 安装 → 定制，而不是从头造轮子。

官方技能库

Anthropic 官方技能库（github.com/anthropics/skills）是质量最高的起点。它自己的定义说得很好：

“技能是包含指令、脚本和资源的文件夹，Claude 会动态加载它们，以提升在专业任务上的表现。”

分类 示例
文档处理 docx、pdf、pptx、xlsx
创意/设计 algorithmic-art、canvas-design、slack-gif-creator
开发 frontend-design、mcp-builder、webapp-testing
企业沟通 brand-guidelines、internal-comms
元技能 skill-creator（一个用来创建技能的技能）

Vercel 技能库（github.com/vercel-labs/skills）专注于 React/Next.js/AI SDK 生态，如果那是你的技术栈，它将非常有价值。

Skills CLI

Vercel 还提供了一个 CLI，相当于技能界的 npm——在终端里搜索、安装和管理技能：

入门时最值得先装的两个：

skill-creator 是一个”元技能”：告诉它你想要什么，它会引导你创建一个结构规范的 SKILL.md 和目录结构。find-skills 则帮你在不知道有什么可用的时候发现现成的技能。这两个都强烈推荐新手安装。

社区技能库

除了官方库，社区已经聚合了数千个技能：

仓库 规模 亮点
alirezarezvani/claude-skills 235+ 9 大领域，25 个”POWERFUL”级进阶技能
ComposioHQ/awesome-claude-skills 127+ 10 大分类，59 个 SaaS 集成技能
travisvn/awesome-claude-skills 精选 社区投票选出的短名单

聚合平台则免去了”逐个翻仓库”的痛苦：skills.sh（约 4.8 万个技能）和 SkillsMP（约 90 万个技能）让你可以按分类和关键词搜索，并一键安装。

安装前的安全检查

技能是一组 _AI 将会执行的指令_——而恶意技能可能包含危险操作。在使用任何第三方技能之前，先做一次快速安全检查：

维度 检查什么 示例
安全性 有危险命令吗？有数据外传吗？ 留意 rm -rf、指向外部主机的 curl
维护状况 最近有更新吗？作者活跃吗？ 超过 6 个月无人维护就要警惕
文档 SKILL.md 是否清晰、有示例？ 文档糟糕往往意味着质量低下
兼容性 与你的工具版本匹配吗？ 查看 frontmatter 的 tools 字段
来源可信度 官方 / 知名组织 / 个人？Star 数如何？ 优先选择官方和高 Star 仓库

黄金法则：

永远不要盲目安装技能。使用前先读它的 SKILL.md 和所有 scripts/——检查是否有网络调用和文件删除操作。官方库优先，高 Star 社区仓库其次，不知名的个人仓库最后。

将技能融入你的工作流

放在文件夹里的技能什么也做不了，直到 AI 知道要去用它。在 Claude Code 中有两种常见的接入方式：

方式一——在 CLAUDE.md 中引用它（推荐）。 列出你的技能，让 AI 在合适的任务中加载合适的技能：

方式二——把它暴露为斜杠命令。 在 .claude/commands/ 中放一个触发文件，就能通过 /skill-name 直接调用某个技能：

对其他工具而言思路是一样的——技能的规则成为项目级上下文。比如在 Cursor 中，你可以把技能的核心规则转写成一个 .cursor/rules/*.mdc 文件。

迭代与版本管理

技能不是”写一次、忘一辈子”的东西。要像对待代码一样对待它：

  • 每次使用后都迭代。 记下 AI 做得好的地方（保留）和做错的地方（加一条更明确的指令）。漏掉了某个边界情况？把它补进错误处理部分。
  • 用 Git 做版本管理。 你的技能目录就是代码，所以要像代码一样提交：

一旦技能被提交到共享仓库，每个拉取代码的人都会获得同样的工作流。这才是真正的回报：最佳实践不再是口口相传的部落知识，而是可版本化、可审查的文件。

最佳实践

一份简短的清单，按你应当应用的顺序排列：

  1. 从最小化开始。 对于简单规则，一个 SKILL.md 胜过一个完整能力包。只有当具体需求出现时才添加目录。
  2. 重复第三次时就技能化。 如果类似的提示词你已经写了三遍，这就是该搭建技能的信号。
  3. 优先使用官方库。 不要重复造 pdf、docx 或 frontend-design 的轮子——直接安装然后定制。
  4. 安装前先阅读。 审查每一个第三方的 SKILL.md 和 scripts/，排查危险命令。
  5. 模板胜过描述。 相比文字叙述，模板文件能更可靠地传达你想要的输出形态。
  6. 把规则放进 references/。 当 AI 必须遵循_你的_标准时，把这些标准写进参考文档，而不是留在你的脑子里。
  7. 用 Git 做版本管理。 像代码一样提交技能，让它们可共享、可审查、可回滚。

常见问题

问：每个技能都真的需要完整的文件夹结构吗？

不需要。很多技能只有一个 SKILL.md，别无他物。用能解决问题的最简单结构——上面的决策指南展示了何时该添加哪些组成部分。

问：SKILL.md 中的 frontmatter 是必需的吗？

不是，它是可选的。它主要在智能体系统需要按 trigger 和 description 自动发现和匹配技能时才重要，这样可以避免把完整指令加载进每一个会话。

问：resources/ 和 references/ 的实际区别是什么？

resources/ 存放直接用于产出结果的_物料_（模板、示例、配置）。references/ 存放 AI 为了做出正确决策而阅读的_知识_（标准、检查清单、API 文档）。前者会被复制进输出；后者只供查阅。

问：怎么让 Claude Code 真正用上我的技能？

在 CLAUDE.md 中引用它，让 AI 在匹配的任务中加载它；或者在 .claude/commands/ 中添加一个触发文件，把它作为斜杠命令调用。

问：技能和 Cursor Rules 是一回事吗？

不完全是，但它们是”表亲”。两者都是”把经验沉淀为可复用的上下文”。Cursor Rules（*.mdc）是项目级的行为指令，而技能是一个更结构化、自包含的能力包，带有脚本和资源。你可以把技能的核心规则转写成一个 Rules 文件。

问：我怎么知道一个第三方技能是否安全？

安装前先阅读它的 SKILL.md 和所有 scripts/，检查是否有危险命令（rm -rf）或数据外传行为（指向外部主机的 curl）。优先选择官方库和高 Star 仓库，并先在一个一次性项目里测试。

问：技能可以调用外部工具吗？

可以。技能可以调用 MCP（Model Context Protocol）服务器来获得额外能力——比如一个部署技能可以调用 GitHub MCP 服务器来创建 PR。但请把 MCP 当作进阶话题；先掌握基础技能。

问：技能和 MCP 有什么区别？

它们是互补的。技能定义_做什么、怎么做_（流程和规则）；MCP 提供_新能力_（把 AI 连接到外部服务）。你可以两者结合使用——一个调用 MCP 所提供工具的技能。

总结

如果说与 AI 对话是下达口头命令，那么技能就是把打印好的操作手册交到它手上。整篇文章可以浓缩为三个习惯：

  1. 把重复的操作技能化。 每个你敲过三遍的提示词都值得变成一个技能。一致性、效率和可复用性都会随之免费获得。
  2. 用可行的最简结构。 从一个 SKILL.md 开始；只有当具体需求出现时才添加 resources/config/、scripts/、resources/template/ 或 references/——绝不提前。
  3. 先借用，再自建。 从 Anthropic 和 Vercel 的官方库安装，审查所有第三方内容，定制而不是重新发明。

其余的都是细节：

主题 一句话要点
是什么 技能是可复用的指令集——一份菜谱/SOP，而不是一次性提示词
结构 SKILL.md 是必需的；scripts/、resources/、references/ 是可选的
一致性 每次运行都遵循同一标准，不同于每次重写的提示词
配置 把固定格式放进 resources/config/，不要硬编码在指令里
校验 把真实逻辑封装进 scripts/，让 AI 调用而不是重新推导
标准 把_你的_规则放进 references/，让审计变得确定而非泛泛
来源 官方库优先，社区仓库其次，不知名的个人仓库最后
维护 每次使用后迭代，并用 Git 对技能做版本管理

从小处开始：为你重复最多的那个提示词写一个 SKILL.md，把它接入 CLAUDE.md，然后用上一次。这第一个技能教会你的东西，会比这篇文章剩下的所有内容加起来还多。

entry.title: Design Patterns
entry.content:
1. Introduction
    • Types of Design Patterns
    • Key Characteristics of Design Patterns
  2. Creational Patterns
    • Factory Pattern
    • Abstract Factory Pattern
    • Builder Pattern
    • Singleton Pattern
  3. Structural Patterns
    • Adapter Pattern
    • Bridge Pattern
    • Composite Pattern
    • Decorator Pattern
    • Facade Pattern
    • Flyweight Pattern
    • Proxy Pattern
  4. Behavioral Patterns
    • Observer Pattern
    • Iterator Pattern
    • Command Pattern
    • Strategy Pattern
    • State Pattern

Introduction

A design pattern is not a rigid structure to be transplanted directly into source code. Rather, it is a description or a template for solving a particular type of problem that can be deployed in many different situations.Design patterns can be viewed as formalized best practices that the programmer may use to solve common problems when designing a software application or system. Expert object-oriented software engineers use these best practices to write more structured, manageable, and scalable code. Design patterns provide a standard terminology and are specific to particular scenarios and problems.

Object-oriented design patterns typically show relationships and interactions between classes or objects, without specifying the final application classes or objects that are involved.[citation needed] Patterns that imply mutable state may be unsuited for functional programming languages. Some patterns can be rendered unnecessary in languages that have built-in support for solving the problem they are trying to solve, and object-oriented patterns are not necessarily suitable for non-object-oriented languages.

Types of Design Patterns

  • Creational Patterns
  • Structural Patterns
  • Behavioral Patterns

Key Characteristics of Design Patterns

  • Reusability: Patterns can be applied to different projects and problems, saving time and effort in solving similar issues.
  • Standardization: They provide a shared language and understanding among developers, helping in communication and collaboration.
  • Efficiency: By using these popular patterns, developers can avoid finding the solution to same recurring problems, which leads to faster development.
  • Flexibility: Patterns are abstract solutions/templates that can be adapted to fit various scenarios and requirements.

Creational Patterns

Core Purpose: Encapsulate object creation logic to decouple object creation from usage.

Factory Pattern


Definition: Uses a factory class to encapsulate object creation, hiding implementation details.
Case: Creating different payment methods in an e-commerce platform.

Abstract Factory


The Abstract Factory Pattern is a creational design pattern that provides an interface for creating families of related or dependent objects without specifying their concrete classes. It encapsulates a group of individual factories that have a common theme, ensuring product compatibility and decoupling client code from implementation details.
Core Concepts:

  1. Abstract Factory: Defines interfaces for creating abstract products.
  2. Concrete Factories: Implement the abstract factory to produce specific product families.
  3. Abstract Products: Declare interfaces for a type of product.
  4. Concrete Products: Implement the abstract product interfaces, created by concrete factories.
  5. Client: Uses the abstract factory and products without depending on concrete classes.

UML Diagram:

Case: Cross-platform UI components (Windows vs. macOS)

Use Cases：

  • Cross-platform Applications: As shown in the example above.
  • Game Development: Creating different enemy types, weapons, or environments.
  • Database Access: Switching between SQL Server, MySQL, etc.
  • UI Frameworks: Generating themed components (light/dark mode).

Builder Pattern


The Builder Pattern is a creational design pattern that separates the construction of a complex object from its representation. This allows the same construction process to create different representations, making it ideal for objects with multiple optional parameters or complex assembly steps.
Core Concepts:

  1. Product: The complex object being constructed (e.g., a car, user profile).
  2. Abstract Builder: Defines an interface for building parts of the product.
  3. Concrete Builder: Implements the builder interface to construct specific product variations.
  4. Director: Controls the construction process, using the builder to assemble the product step-by-step.

UML Diagram:

Case:Building a computer with optional components (CPU, GPU, RAM).

Output:

Use Cases:

  1. Complex Objects with Many Parameters: E.g., cars, user profiles, or API requests with optional fields.
  2. Object Assembly with Order Dependency: When parts must be added in a specific sequence (e.g., initializing components before final assembly).
  3. Fluent Interfaces: Commonly used to create fluent APIs for readability (e.g., StringBuilder in .NET).

Singleton Pattern


The Singleton Pattern is a creational design pattern that ensures a class has only one instance and provides a global point of access to it. This pattern is useful for systems where exactly one instance is needed to coordinate actions across the system, such as a database connection pool, logging service, or configuration manager.
Core Concepts:

  1. Private Constructor: Prevents direct instantiation of the class from outside.
  2. Static Instance: Holds the single instance of the class.
  3. Public Static Accessor: Provides global access to the instance.
    UML Diagram: Implementation Variations:
  4. Basic Singleton (Not Thread-Safe) Issue: Not thread-safe. Multiple threads can create instances simultaneously in a multi-threaded environment.
  5. Thread-Safe Singleton (Double-Checked Locking)
  6. Lazy Initialization with Lazy Use Cases:
  • Logging Services: Centralized logging to avoid file conflicts.
  • Database Connection Pools: Reuse connections to optimize performance.
  • Configuration Managers: Load and manage application settings.
  • Graphics Managers: Control rendering or display resources.

Structural Patterns

Structural design patterns explain how to assemble objects and classes into larger structures, while keeping these structures flexible and efficient.

Adapter Pattern


The Adapter Pattern is a structural design pattern that allows objects with incompatible interfaces to collaborate. It acts as a bridge between two incompatible interfaces, converting the interface of one class into another interface clients expect. This pattern is useful for integrating legacy code, third-party libraries, or mismatched components without modifying their original structure.
Core Concepts:

  1. Target: The interface that the client expects to interact with.
  2. Adaptee: The existing class with an incompatible interface.
  3. Adapter: Converts the adaptee’s interface into the target interface via composition or inheritance.
    UML Diagram：
  4. Object Adapter (Composition) Usage:
  5. Class Adapter (Inheritance) Note: Class Adapter requires multiple inheritance (not supported in C#), so this example uses composition instead.
    Use Cases:
  6. Legacy System Integration: Connect new code with outdated APIs.
  7. Third-Party Libraries: Adapt external libraries to match your application’s interface.
  8. Data Format Conversion: Transform data between incompatible formats (e.g., XML to JSON).
  9. Cross-Platform Compatibility: Adapt platform-specific APIs to a common interface.
    Real-World Examples:
  • .NET Framework: StreamReader adapts a Stream to a text reader.
  • Java: java.util.Arrays.asList() adapts an array to a List.
  • Web APIs: Converting REST API responses to internal data models.

Bridge Pattern


The Bridge Pattern is a structural design pattern that decouples an abstraction from its implementation, allowing both to vary independently. It achieves this by separating the hierarchical abstraction (what the system does) from the implementation (how it does it), connected via a bridge interface. This pattern is particularly useful for avoiding a “class explosion” when dealing with multiple dimensions of variability.
Core Concepts:

  1. Abstraction: Defines the high-level interface and depends on the implementation interface.
  2. Refined Abstraction: Extends the abstraction without affecting the implementation.
  3. Implementor: Defines the interface for the implementation classes.
  4. Concrete Implementor: Provides the concrete implementation.
    UML Diagram: Implementation Example
    Scenario: Rendering shapes (circle, square) in different formats (vector, raster).

Use Cases:

  • Cross-Platform Applications: Separate platform-specific implementations from business logic.
  • GUI Frameworks: Render UI components in different styles (e.g., Windows vs. macOS).
  • Database Drivers: Connect to different databases (SQL Server, MySQL) using a common interface.
  • Game Development: Render graphics using different APIs (DirectX, OpenGL).

Composite Pattern


The Composite Pattern is a structural design pattern that lets you compose objects into tree structures to represent part-whole hierarchies. It allows clients to treat individual objects (leaf nodes) and compositions of objects (composite nodes) uniformly, simplifying code by treating all nodes through a common interface.
Core Concepts:

  1. Component: Defines the common interface for both leaf and composite nodes.
  2. Leaf: Represents individual objects (no children).
  3. Composite: Manages child components, implementing the component interface for child-related operations(add, remove and get).
  4. Client: Interacts with components through the common interface, unaware of whether they are leaves or composites.
    UML Diagram: Use case: A file system with directories (composites) and files (leaves). Output: Use Cases:
  • File Systems: Directories (composites) and files (leaves).
  • GUI Toolkits: Containers (e.g., panels) and widgets (e.g., buttons).
  • Organization Charts: Departments (composites) and employees (leaves).
  • Tree-Based Data Structures: XML/JSON parsing, syntax trees.

Decorator Pattern


The Decorator Pattern is a structural design pattern that lets you attach new behaviors to objects dynamically by placing these objects inside special wrapper classes. It provides a flexible alternative to subclassing for extending functionality, allowing behavior to be added or removed at runtime.
Core Concepts:

  1. Component: Defines the common interface for objects that can have decorations.
  2. Concrete Component: Implements the base functionality of the component.
  3. Decorator: Maintains a reference to a component and implements the component interface.
  4. Concrete Decorators: Add specific behaviors to the component by overriding methods.

Use case: Coffee shop where drinks (components) can be decorated with additives (decorators).

Output:

Use Cases:
GUI Components: Adding borders, scroll bars, or tooltips to widgets.
I/O Streams: Wrapping streams with buffering, encryption, or compression.
Logging: Adding timestamps, metadata, or formatting to log messages.
Security: Applying authentication or authorization layers to requests.

Facade Pattern


The Facade Pattern is a structural design pattern that provides a simplified interface to a complex system of classes, libraries, or APIs. It hides the underlying complexity and exposes only high-level functionality, making the system easier to use and maintain. This pattern is commonly used to decouple clients from intricate subsystems.
Core Concepts:

  1. Facade: Provides a simplified interface to the subsystem.
  2. Subsystem Classes: Implement complex functionality but are unaware of the facade.
  3. Client: Interacts with the facade instead of directly accessing subsystem classes.
    UML Diagram Uase case: A home theater system with multiple components (amplifier, DVD player, projector). Output: Use Cases:
  • Complex APIs: Simplify third-party libraries (e.g., cloud storage APIs).
  • Legacy Systems: Provide a modern interface to outdated code.
  • Cross-Layer Communication: Bridge different layers in an application (e.g., UI and business logic).
  • Testing: Create facades to mock complex subsystems during unit testing.

Flyweight Pattern


The Flyweight Pattern is a structural design pattern that minimizes memory usage by sharing as much data as possible between similar objects. It achieves this by separating intrinsic (shared) state from extrinsic (context-specific) state, allowing objects to be reused across different contexts. This pattern is particularly useful for optimizing memory when dealing with large numbers of similar objects.
Core Concepts:

  1. Flyweight: Defines the interface for shared objects, managing intrinsic state.
  2. Concrete Flyweight: Implements the flyweight interface and stores intrinsic state.
  3. Flyweight Factory: Manages a pool of flyweight objects, ensuring they are shared and reused.
  4. Client: Holds extrinsic state and uses the flyweight factory to obtain flyweight instances.

Complete code of the flyweight design pattern:

Use Cases:

  • Graphics Systems: Reuse shared textures, sprites, or glyphs.
  • Game Development: Share common assets (e.g., terrain tiles, enemy models).
  • Document Editors: Reuse characters, fonts, or formatting styles.
  • Database Connections: Pool and reuse connection objects.

Proxy Pattern


The Proxy Pattern is a structural design pattern that provides a surrogate or placeholder for another object to control access to it. Proxies act as intermediaries between clients and real objects, allowing additional functionality (e.g., lazy loading, access control, logging) without changing the real object’s interface.
Core Concepts

  1. Subject: Defines the common interface for the RealSubject and Proxy.
  2. RealSubject: Implements the subject interface, containing the actual business logic.
  3. Proxy: Maintains a reference to the RealSubject and controls access to it.
  4. Client: Interacts with the Proxy as if it were the RealSubject.
    UML Diagram: Use case:A high-resolution image loader with lazy initialization. Output: Use Cases:
  • Remote Proxies: Hide network communication details (e.g., .NET Remoting).
  • Virtual Proxies: Delay expensive operations (e.g., lazy loading images).
  • Protection Proxies: Control access based on permissions (e.g., user roles).
  • Smart References: Add additional behavior when accessing an object (e.g., reference counting).

Behavioral Patterns

Observer Pattern

The Observer Pattern is a behavioral design pattern that establishes a one-to-many dependency between objects. When one object (the subject) changes state, all its dependents (the observers) are notified and updated automatically. This pattern is ideal for implementing event-driven systems, where multiple components need to react to state changes.
Core Concepts:

  1. Subject: Manages a list of observers and notifies them of state changes.
  2. Observer: Defines an interface for receiving updates from the subject.
  3. Concrete Subject: Implements the subject interface and stores state that interests observers.
  4. Concrete Observer: Implements the observer interface and maintains a reference to the concrete subject.

Output:

Real-World Examples:

  • Java Event Listeners: ActionListener in Swing components.
  • .NET Events: System.EventHandler and event subscribers.
  • RxJava/Rx.NET: Reactive Extensions use the observer pattern for asynchronous streams.

Iterator Pattern


The Iterator Pattern is a behavioral design pattern that provides a way to access the elements of an aggregate object (e.g., a collection) sequentially without exposing its underlying representation. It decouples the traversal logic from the collection, allowing different traversal algorithms or multiple traversals simultaneously.
Core Concepts:

  1. Iterator: Defines an interface for accessing and traversing elements.
  2. Concrete Iterator: Implements the iterator interface, tracking the current position in the collection.
  3. Aggregate: Defines an interface for creating an iterator.
  4. Concrete Aggregate: Implements the aggregate interface to return a concrete iterator.
    Use case: A custom collection (name repository) with a forward iterator. Output: Use Cases:
  • Custom Collections: Traverse non-standard data structures (e.g., trees, graphs).
  • Database Results: Iterate over query results without exposing underlying data.
  • File System Navigation: Traverse directories and files.
  • Parallel Processing: Split traversal tasks across multiple threads.

Command Pattern


The Command Pattern is a behavioral design pattern that turns a request into a stand-alone object, containing all information about the request. This decouples the sender (invoker) from the receiver (executor), allowing requests to be parameterized, queued, logged, or undone.
Core Concepts:

  1. Command: Defines an interface for executing an operation.
  2. Concrete Command: Implements the command interface, binding a receiver to an action.
  3. Invoker: Asks the command to carry out the request.
  4. Receiver: Knows how to perform the operation associated with the command.
  5. Client: Creates a concrete command and sets its receiver.
    Uase case: A remote control (invoker) that can turn on/off a light (receiver) using commands. Use Cases:
  • GUI Buttons: Map button clicks to specific actions (e.g., “Save” command).
  • Undo/Redo Systems: Track and reverse user actions in applications.
  • Transaction Management: Group commands into atomic operations.
  • Networking: Send commands over a network (e.g., remote procedure calls).

Real-World Examples:

  • Java Thread Pool: Runnable and Callable interfaces act as commands.
  • .NET Delegate: Encapsulates a method call as an object.
  • GUI Frameworks: Action classes (e.g., javax.swing.Action in Java).

Strategy Pattern


The Strategy Pattern is a behavioral design pattern that defines a family of algorithms, encapsulates each one, and makes them interchangeable. It lets the algorithm vary independently from the clients that use it, promoting flexibility and maintainability.
Core Concepts:

  1. Strategy: Defines the common interface for all concrete algorithms.
  2. Concrete Strategies: Implement the strategy interface with specific algorithms.
  3. Context: Maintains a reference to a strategy and uses it to perform a task.
  4. Client: Configures the context with a specific strategy.
